extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetic theory (readers of Wordsworth/Coleridge-era criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for choosing diction, imagery, sentence-order, and rhetorical devices in metrical (verse) composition — especially how metre interacts with passion, volition, and the language of prose or rustic speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre should be accompanied by the natural language of excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: “As the elements of metre owe their existence to a state of increased excitement, so the metre itself should be accompanied by the natural language of excitement.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge argues that because metre originates in a checked/regulated state of passion, the diction of metrical poetry should reflect the heightened, excited language appropriate to that emotional state. He cites the example of intense repetitive usages (e.g., Deborah’s song) as legitimate beauties of passionate expression. Conversely, mere colloquial vacillations or filler-phrases of an unfurnished mind do not serve as poetic ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traces of present volition must be discernible in metrical language
rubrics_metrics.description: “The traces of present volition should throughout the metrical language be proportionately discernible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because metre is an artificial organization (a voluntary act) imposed on passion to blend delight with emotion, the poet’s conscious shaping (choices of order, emphasis, and figure) should be perceptible in verse. The metrical language must therefore show an interpenetration of spontaneous feeling and deliberate craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union/interpenetration of passion and will
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be “not only a partnership, but a union; an interpenetration of passion and of will, of spontaneous impulse and of voluntary purpose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good metrical poetry reconciles and manifests both spontaneous excitement and the poet’s self-restraint/judgment. The aesthetic effect depends on this coexistence; one without the other makes the metre inappropriate or ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect greater frequency of picturesque and vivifying figures in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre tends to produce “a more frequent employment of picturesqe and vivifying language, than would be natural in any other case.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the tacit compact between poet and reader that metre will provide heightened pleasure, the critic should expect a higher density of figures of speech, epithets, and lively images in poetry than in ordinary prose. This frequency is proper when it serves the metrical/passional purpose, but becomes a fault when used gratuitously or without fitting matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre requires appropriate intellectual and emotional matter
rubrics_metrics.description: “Metre in itself is simply a stimulant of the attention... Where, therefore, correspondent food and appropriate matter are not provided for the attention and feelings thus roused there must needs be a disappointment felt.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic should judge whether the poem’s thoughts, images, and emotional material match the stimulant effect of metre. Metre without suitable substance (ideas, images, feeling) produces a sense of emptiness or mismatch; poets should not rely on metre alone to sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in a language different from prose when employing metre
rubrics_metrics.description: “I write in metre, because I am about to use a language different from that of prose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The use of metre must be justified by a corresponding departure from prose-style diction and organization. If the poet merely uses prose diction in verse, the metrical form is unjustified and likely to feel awkward or prosaic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some expressions/orders suitable to prose are disproportionate in poetry and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist “modes of expression, a construction, and an order of sentences” that are fitting in serious prose but “disproportionate and heterogeneous in metrical poetry; and, vice versa.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and poets must assess fit: sentence-order, constructions, and kinds/frequencies of figures that are correct for prose may be unseemly in verse. Coleridge illustrates with Daniel’s ‘prosaic’ lines and with Wordsworth’s colloquial stanzas that feel ill-assorted to rhyme and metre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid illogical, arbitrary, or novelty-seeking diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet who uses “an illogical diction, or a style fitted to excite only the low and changeable pleasure of wonder by means of groundless novelty, substitutes a language of folly and vanity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should not sacrifice sense and coherence for mere oddity or novelty. Groundless or capricious phrasing that shocks through novelty rather than conveys meaning is an anti-pattern; such diction undermines poetic seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not slavishly adopt rustic or low dialect without adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempt to “imitate, and, as far as is possible, to adopt the very language of men” (i.e., the real language of rustic life) is impracticable and often useless; selection implies prior possession of the language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge contends the poet must possess and select from language, including order and syntax, rather than mechanically transplanting village speech. Rustic phraseology must be cleansed of provincialisms and adapted (omissions/changes) before serving poetic ends; otherwise the diction will be inconsistent across regions and unsuited to metrical needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images and epithets must be congruous with good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines are faulty not for being poetic but for “convey[ing] incongruous images; because [they] confound the cause and the effect; the real thing with the personified representative of the thing; in short, because [they] differ from the language of good sense!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of personification, epithets, or mythological references must preserve logical congruence and clarity. Coleridge cites the objectionable ‘reddening Phoebus lifts his golden fire’ as confounding images and notes that hackneyed or anachronistic personifications are accidental faults, not necessarily failures of poetry per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre is not justification for mere mnemonic or archaic ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although metre historically aided recollection and preservation, that alone does not justify metrical choice for poor or trivial matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic should not excuse weak thought, trivial incidents, or prosaic substance merely because they are metrical. Coleridge contrasts popular prose tales that survived without metre to argue that metre is not a sufficient cause of literary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition demands unity: parts must be assimilated to essential parts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a “high spiritual instinct... to seek unity by harmonious adjustment, and thus establishing the principle that all the parts of an organized whole must be assimilated to the more important and essential parts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems should aim for harmonious unity: subordinate elements must be adjusted to the central purpose or dominant parts. This principle supports the argument that poetic diction, structure, and metre should be consistent with the poem’s chief aims and not jar with them.
